Whenever the data is temporal and you will deploy the model to predict future events. A random split lets rows from the future land in the training set, which leaks information that wouldn't be available at prediction time and inflates your metrics. A time-based split reproduces the real task, exposes distribution drift/non-stationarity, and gives an honest estimate of deployment performance. It's essentially the idea behind time-series cross-validation.

Prompt caching lets the provider reuse a large, stable prefix instead of reprocessing it, cutting cost and latency on repeat requests. It works by prefix match: everything from the start of the prompt up to the first differing byte is reused, so cache-friendly design puts stable content first - a frozen system prompt, a deterministic tool list - and only appends new content at the end.

ROC is the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve and AUC is the Area Under it. The curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate as you vary the decision threshold. AUC summarizes ranking quality independent of any single threshold and equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative.

After SFT the model follows instructions but can still be unhelpful, verbose, or unsafe. RLHF aligns it to human preferences: humans compare several candidate responses and rank which is better; those comparisons train a reward model that scores responses, and the LLM is then optimized to maximize that reward, i.e., to produce answers people prefer. This improves helpfulness, safety, tone, and honesty beyond what SFT alone achieves.

A token is a sub-word unit produced by the tokenizer; the model reads and generates text one token at a time over a fixed vocabulary of tens of thousands of tokens. Sub-word tokenization is the sweet spot between characters and whole words: it keeps the embedding/output matrices bounded while composing rare words from pieces, so nothing is truly OOV, and it generalizes across languages.

SVMs are distance- and inner-product-based: the margin and kernels like the RBF depend on the geometric distance between points. If features are on very different scales, the large-magnitude feature dominates the distance computation and the SVM essentially ignores the smaller-scale features, and the C penalty is applied unevenly. Standardizing or min-max scaling puts features on comparable footing so the margin reflects all of them.

ANN finds vectors that are close enough to the query far faster than exact search. Exact KNN scans every vector, O per query, which collapses at millions or billions of vectors. ANN builds an index offline so a query only explores a small candidate subset instead of the whole set, trading a little accuracy for a big speedup.

Logistic regression models the probability that an observation belongs to the positive class as a function of its features, by passing a linear combination of the features through the sigmoid function. Under the hood it is a regression: it fits a linear model to the log-odds of the target and produces a continuous probability between 0 and 1.

Naive RAG concatenates every retrieved chunk, so context grows fast and quality drops. The pattern is retrieve more, keep less. First rewrite the user request together with the current task state into a sharper query. Then retrieve a broad candidate set - say top-k of 12 - to get high recall. Then rerank and keep only the best handful, maybe the top 4, for precision.

That's the classic signature of multicollinearity. When predictors are highly correlated, the design matrix is near-singular, so infinitely many coefficient combinations fit almost equally well; least squares picks one with huge variance, and the estimates become unstable, can flip sign, and are not individually interpretable, even though overall prediction and R2 may be fine.
